summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that helps mission planners, teachers, and the public evaluate Moon landing sites, especially near the south pole. Users pick a location and a date, and the app shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon—revealing whether solar power and direct communication are available, and how long until sunset or Earthset.
It matters because at the south pole, small changes in location or date drastically alter lighting and Earth visibility, and missions often slip. Current tools are highly technical and make comparing scenarios hard.
We tackled the challenge by turning NASA data into clear visuals: a 360° topographic horizon using LRO LOLA, 29.5-day charts, a 3D lunar globe, a landing simulator, and a side-by-side comparator. Positions come from JPL Horizons, with a local fallback. Technical and educational modes, in Spanish and English, cater to different experience levels.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that helps you evaluate landing sites on the Moon, especially near the south pole. You pick a site and a date, and the app shows where the Sun and Earth are relative to the horizon, so you can tell whether there will be solar power and direct communication, and how long until sunset or Earthset. It includes a 360° horizon view, charts covering a full 29.5-day lunar cycle, a 3D lunar globe, a landing simulator, and 7 curated sites from NASA, CLPS, Apollo, and the CSA, plus the option to compare scenarios.

It runs on a Next.js API route that queries NASA JPL Horizons to get the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth from the chosen spot. If Horizons doesn’t respond, a local engine calculates the positions using libration and orbital variations. Those are then compared against the horizon, without atmospheric refraction, using topographic profiles from LRO LOLA, and React draws everything with Canvas, SVG, and Three.js. It also links to Moon Trek and QuickMap so you can look at the terrain in detail.

The benefit is that you can find out in seconds whether a site and date are viable, and compare alternatives when a mission gets delayed. It's useful for planners, teachers, and anyone interested in lunar exploration, and it shows why the south pole is so tricky. We hope to bring NASA’s technical data closer to everyone, support mission planning for programs like CLPS and Artemis, and down the road add more sites, fine-tune the topography, and validate against Horizons and QuickMap.

We built it with TypeScript, Python 3, CSS with Tailwind, HTML5 Canvas and SVG, a Batch/PowerShell launcher, and JSON for the configuration and the PWA manifest. The main libraries are Next.js 13.5.6, React 18.3.1, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, and Tailwind CSS. The data comes from JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, the NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit, LROC QuickMap, and LRO LOLA.
